```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(gpcseq)
```

## Plan the looks and the test

Should a trial stop when treatment–control comparisons can still change with follow-up? Choose the clinical comparison, the scheduled calendar looks and the spending rule before monitoring begins. The length of `looks` gives the number of analyses, including the final analysis. For example, `looks = c(12, 24, 36)` specifies two interim looks and a final analysis at month 36. By default, the package uses O’Brien–Fleming-like spending at a two-sided level of 0.05. It evaluates the spending function at each look’s calendar time divided by the planned final calendar time. These are prespecified spending fractions, not estimates of statistical information. An analyst can instead supply planned fractions or the cumulative alpha at each look.

For the worked trial, we use one interim and one final analysis. At each look we compare each treatment patient with each control patient through their shared follow-up. Death settles a comparison; while both patients are alive, fewer admissions wins and a later last admission breaks a count tie. Under the null, treatment wins and losses are equally probable throughout follow-up.

```{r plan}
trial <- gpc_design(looks = c(1, 2), method = "shared")
trial$design$spending                 # Cumulative alpha at the two looks
```

The O’Brien–Fleming-like rule reserves most of the error for the final analysis. For more early spending, use `spending = "pocock"`. The Kim–DeMets power and Hwang–Shih–DeCani families allow the curve’s shape to be specified; see `?gpc_design`.

## At the interim look: stop or continue?

Six patients enter at calendar time 0. The following function supplies the records available at each look. It extends the four patients in `gpc_example()` with a treated patient admitted at 0.25 and an admission-free control; both remain alive. In a staggered-entry trial, supply only patients enrolled by that look, with event times measured since each patient's entry.

```{r data-cuts}
trial_cut <- function(k) {
  x <- gpc_example(k)
  patients <- rbind(x$patients,
    data.frame(id = c("T3", "C3"), arm = c(1L, 0L), entry = 0,
               followup = k, death = FALSE, state0 = "well"))
  events <- rbind(x$events,
    data.frame(id = "T3", time = .25, type = "hospitalization", value = NA_real_))
  gpc_trial_data(patients, events = list(admission = events[c("id", "time")]))
}

trial <- gpc_update(trial, data = trial_cut(1))
gpc_results(trial)[, c("look", "estimate", "se", "z", "critical", "spent", "action")]
```

At time 1 there are five wins, two losses and two ties. The mean signed score is $(5-2)/9=1/3$. Dividing by its standard error, 0.416, gives $Z_1=0.802$. At the halfway look the default rule spends 0.00557 in total over both tails, giving a critical value of 2.772. The trial continues.

## At the final look: use the updated histories

At time 1, T2 and C2 were both alive. T2 won because C2 had been admitted and T2 had not. T2 dies at 1.5 while C2 remains alive, reversing that pair's score. The first-look decision stands; the final analysis uses the updated histories of all six patients.

```{r final-look}
trial <- gpc_update(trial, data = trial_cut(2))
gpc_results(trial)[, c("look", "estimate", "se", "z", "critical", "spent", "action")]
V <- gpc_covariance(trial)
cov2cor(V)
```

At the final look there are four wins, four losses and one tie, so $Z_2=0$. To set the final boundary, the package matches each patient's influence at the two looks. Their cross-products give the estimated covariance of the two scores and a correlation of 0.777 between their standardized statistics. With this correlation, a final boundary of 1.973 leaves probability $0.05-0.00557=0.04443$ under the null of **continuing at the first look and rejecting at the second**. Neither boundary was crossed; the trial ends without rejection.

For a trial with more looks, call `gpc_update()` once per scheduled look while the trial is open. A deferred look spends no error. The next usable look spends the difference between its planned cumulative level and the amount already spent.

## When the question concerns a common follow-up horizon

The shared-window test above uses a different observation window for each pair. If the protocol targets a treatment effect through a specified duration since entry, keep the same calendar-look workflow and change the estimator. For restricted net benefit, set `method = "ipcw"`; the comparison must be observed through the first death in the pair or the horizon, whichever comes first. Estimated censoring weights account for incomplete observation. For restricted net win time, set `method = "aj"` and supply patients' initial states and observed transitions.

For example, the following design schedules looks at months 12, 24 and 36. At each look the clinical comparison extends at most 24 months since entry, and only as far as at least a quarter of enrollees in each arm have had the opportunity to reach.

```{r maturity-plan}
restricted <- gpc_design(looks = c(12, 24, 36), spending = c(.005, .02, .05),
                         method = "ipcw", maturity = list(p = .25, cap = 24))
```

Suppose 25 of 100 patients in an arm enrolled at least 12 months before a look. All 25 had the opportunity for 12 months of follow-up. If 10 died and five others dropped out before 12 months, only 10 are still under observation at that horizon. The observed deaths can still settle pairwise comparisons. For an IPCW fit, inspect `diagnostics$risk_at_horizon` and `diagnostics$G_at_horizon` in each arm. A look that fails the prespecified support thresholds is skipped.

Even when those thresholds are met, a few patients or events at an early look can make the Gaussian approximation inaccurate. Before fixing the design, simulate trials under the null with the planned enrollment, event rates, and censoring. Apply the full stopping rule to each simulated trial and estimate how often any boundary is crossed and how often a look is skipped. See `vignette("monitoring", package = "gpcseq")` for a worked example of the resulting spending and stopping decisions.
